A mild headline miss — and the wrong number to anchor to.
- The 4-week moving average sits at 195,250 — well below the 225,000 softening threshold and unchanged in trend.
That is the number the Fed watches.
It has not moved.
- Continued claims fell 20,000 to 1,697,000, beating the 1,710,000 consensus by 13,000.
Workers who lost jobs previously are finding new ones.
The reabsorption rate is intact.
- What would change the thesis: a 230,000+ initial print accompanied by continued claims climbing back above 1,750,000 — in the same week.
One of those alone is noise.
Both together reopens the softening conversation.

Though there have been an increasing number of job cut announcements by large companies in recent weeks, including Verizon Communications Inc.
and Amazon.com Inc., there hasn’t been a notable pickup in actual layoffs yet.
Recurring claims have largely trended upward since September and remain near levels last seen when the labor market was recovering from the pandemic.

The weekly claims data are prone to swings around holidays, such as Thanksgiving.

Recent surveys show Americans are increasingly worried about the labor market.
A measure of consumer confidence in November fell by the most in seven months, partially due to more downbeat prospects for finding a job.

Federal Reserve officials lowered interest rates at their last two policy meetings with a focus on bolstering the slowing labor market.
But policymakers are divided on whether to support another cut at their final meeting of the year in December as they attempt to balance that weakening along with inflation which remains elevated.
